headline: Bank of Canada Holds at 2.25% as Latest CPI Snapshot Reads +2.8% and Housing Starts Hold at 279,317 SAAR
executive_summary:
The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on June 10, a second consecutive hold delivered alongside the latest Monetary Policy Report — the decision leaves 1,862 active rate-sensitive construction projects ($284.3B) financing against a Government of Canada curve whose 5-year benchmark sits at 3.04%, the mortgage-renewal anchor for residential and commercial borrowers.28 The next scheduled decision is July 9, sequenced one week after US June payrolls.29

Headline CPI registered +2.8% year-over-year on the latest snapshot, up 0.4 percentage points, with the formal May print scheduled for July 17 — core-trim and core-median both sit at 2.0%, while April component detail recorded energy +28.6% y/y, food +3.8% y/y, and shelter +1.8% y/y.64 Average hourly wage fell 1.4% month-over-month to $37.24 in May, set against the +2.8% headline pace.67

Monthly real GDP declined 0.1% in March 2026, with the April GDP-by-industry release scheduled for June 24 — mining, quarrying and oil-and-gas extraction GDP fell 2.1% month-over-month and manufacturing GDP ran 2.5% below year-ago levels, even as April manufacturing sales rose 4.2% m/m to $77,052.9M.6672 The database tracks 346 active manufacturing projects ($70.0B) and 642 mining/oil-and-gas projects ($263.1B) against those readings.

Unemployment held at 6.6% in May while housing starts rose to 279,317 SAAR, up 6.9% from the April pace of 261,377 — the employment rate stood at 60.7% and participation at 65.0%, with accommodation and food employment up 4.3% m/m against retail down 1.8% m/m.67 April residential building permits fell 5.5% m/m and non-residential permits fell 10.5% m/m, even as starts advanced; the database tracks 272 active residential projects ($41.6B).8144

WTI crude settled at $75.43/bbl, down 6.4% on the week and 21.9% over the month, framing the energy-export picture into next week's data calendar — the price remains above the $74–76 breakeven cluster the cross-reference engine cites for 91 active oil-and-gas projects ($63.2B), and April energy exports rose 9.7% m/m to $19.88B.68 The June 24 April GDP release, the July 9 Bank of Canada decision, and the July 17 CPI print sequence the indicators that will reset this picture.6447

national.analysis:
Monthly real GDP contracted 0.1% in March 2026, down 0.2 percentage points from the +0.1% February pace, according to Statistics Canada — the April GDP-by-industry release is scheduled for June 24 and will carry sectoral detail across all 20 NAICS industries.66 The March decline was led by goods-producing industries: mining, quarrying and oil-and-gas extraction fell 2.1% month-over-month, and on a year-over-year basis manufacturing ran 2.5% below 2025 levels while mining sat 1.5% lower and construction 1.5% lower.

Industry GDP diverged sharply across services in the March reference month — finance and insurance rose 3.6% y/y, information and cultural industries 3.2% y/y, and transportation and warehousing 3.1% y/y, against management of companies and enterprises at -22.7% y/y, a small, volatile aggregate.66 Manufacturing told a two-speed story: GDP -2.5% y/y while April manufacturing sales rose 4.2% m/m to $77,052.9M and wholesale sales rose 2.8% m/m to $138,830.0M.7276 The database tracks 346 active manufacturing projects ($70.0B).

The labour market held its level in May, with unemployment at 6.6% and the employment rate at 60.7% — participation stood at 65.0% and average hourly wage fell 1.4% m/m to $37.24.6770 By industry, accommodation and food employment rose 4.3% m/m while retail employment fell 1.8% m/m. The next Labour Force Survey, covering June, is scheduled for July 3.

The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% on June 10, its second consecutive hold — the decision was paired with the Monetary Policy Report and leaves the 5-year Government of Canada benchmark at 3.04% as the mortgage-renewal anchor for 1,862 active rate-sensitive construction projects ($284.3B).28 Headline CPI registered +2.8% y/y on the latest snapshot with the formal May print due July 17; core-trim and core-median both held at 2.0%.64

Housing starts rose to 279,317 SAAR in May, up 6.9% from the April pace of 261,377, even as April building permits declined — residential permits fell 5.5% m/m and non-residential permits fell 10.5% m/m, and the new housing price index eased 0.4% m/m to 121.1 in April.817444 The database tracks 272 active residential projects ($41.6B). On trade, April merchandise exports reached $66.3B, with energy exports up 9.7% m/m to $19.88B; WTI crude settled at $75.43/bbl, down 6.4% on the week and 21.9% over the month, above the $74–76 breakeven cluster cited for 91 active oil-and-gas projects ($63.2B).68 Capital expenditure intentions for 2026 stand at $401,203M, up 3.7% y/y.78

Across the broader sector map, services GDP held up against goods-producing weakness in the March reference month — retail trade GDP rose 0.8% y/y and wholesale trade 1.0% y/y, real estate, rental and leasing 1.8% y/y, and public administration 1.1% y/y, against arts, entertainment and recreation up 3.5% y/y.66 Household disposable income reached $1,811,968M in Q1 2026, up 0.6% q/q, while the savings rate eased to 3.5% from 3.7%.82 The database tracks 6,485 active projects valued at $1,620.8B, with 135 newly recorded this week, spanning the rate-sensitive construction, residential, and energy pipelines that finance against the indicators above.

provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate stood at 7.0% in the June Labour Force Survey while wage growth decelerated to +2.1% in May, down 2.1 percentage points from +4.2% — the wage slowdown71 sits across employment-sensitive sectors that the project database tracks in volume, including 115 healthcare and 222 infrastructure files15. The 2026 Ontario Budget forecasts 2026 real GDP growth near 1.0% and the unemployment rate easing from 7.7% in 2025 toward 7.4% in 2026.

Housing starts fell 8.4% to 62,735 units SAAR as of June 15, the steepest decline among the large provinces this period — the residential contraction44 runs alongside a budget that adds $111.3B in total infrastructure spending over 2025-26 to 2027-28, up $13.6B from the 2025 FES and including an additional $11.0B in planned transit3. The database tracks 694 Ontario projects, of which 91 qualify above the $500M threshold and total roughly $297.2B; infrastructure (222 files) and transport_logistics (134) are the two largest categories by count.

Ontario CPI registered +2.9% year-over-year on the May reference period — the print73 accompanies a capital pipeline led by the Adaptive Phased Management Deep Geological Repository, the province's largest tracked file at $26.0B in Proposed status15. Agnico Eagle's $14B Ontario mining capital program is Proposed in the Timmins region, while Honda's $15B EV and battery complex is marked Cancelled in the database after an indefinite 2026 suspension.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Infrastructure and transport lead Ontario's tracked pipeline by count — the database records 222 infrastructure and 134 transport_logistics projects, with the Ontario Line and GO Expansion both Under Construction in the Toronto area2. Healthcare (115 files) and the 41 mining files sit in employment-sensitive and commodity-exposed categories; Agnico Eagle's $14B capital program (Proposed) anchors the mining count, while the Cancelled $15B Honda EV complex underscores manufacturing's CAD/USD and auto-sector exposure.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Ontario's labour market carried a 7.0% unemployment rate, a 64.7% participation rate, and a 60.2% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth slowed to +2.1% in May, a 2.1-percentage-point deceleration from +4.2%71. The 2026 Budget notes 2025 added roughly +80,900 net jobs, nearly all private sector, and forecasts a softer 2026 labour market on slower population growth, with employment growth near 0.5%3.
provinces.consumerPulse: Ontario CPI ran at +2.9% year-over-year on the May reference period, the highest among the large provinces this period — the inflation read73 accompanies decelerating wage growth of +2.1%, narrowing the gap between price and pay changes for Ontario households. Housing starts at 62,735 SAAR (-8.4%) point to a residential market cooling against a budget-backed infrastructure and transit build-out.

Rate-sensitive transit and infrastructure plans dominate, while mining and manufacturing files carry commodity and CAD/USD exposure.

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.analysis:
Quebec's unemployment rate held at 5.6% in the June Labour Force Survey while CPI ran at +1.5% year-over-year, the second-lowest provincial inflation rate this period — wage growth71 decelerated to +4.7% in May, down 1.2 percentage points from +5.9%. The province's quarterly provincial accounts (qc_real_gdp at $486,872.7M, qc_nominal_gdp at $652,636M) carry a 2025-10-01 reference period and are cited as such rather than as current-week figures.

Hydro-Quebec reported Q1 2026 net income of $1,850M, down $206M year-over-year, alongside a record quarterly investment of $1.6B — the utility20 launched a financing program exceeding $5B with the Canada Infrastructure Bank and National Bank for Indigenous wind participation and announced five wind partnerships totalling more than 10,000 MW. Its Action Plan 2035 targets $135-160B in investment, and the database tracks 49 Quebec power_energy projects within 95 qualifying files above the $250M threshold totalling roughly $120.3B15.

Quebec's tracked pipeline spans 502 projects, the largest categories by count being education (110), infrastructure (99) and power_energy (49) — Parc eolien zone Chamouchouane ($9.0B, Proposed) ranks among the largest tracked wind files15, while the Canada-Quebec federal infrastructure funding transfer ($10B, Proposed) and the Montreal Metro Blue Line Extension ($4.9B, Under Construction, 2031 target) anchor the rate-sensitive transit pipeline50.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and education lead Quebec's tracked count, with Hydro-Quebec anchoring energy-sector exposure — the database records 49 power_energy and 110 education files3. Hydro-Quebec's record $1.6B quarterly investment, Action Plan 2035 ($135-160B target), and five wind partnerships exceeding 10,000 MW concentrate capital in renewables; copper and electrical-equipment input costs flow through to the wind and grid capital plans2.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Quebec recorded a 5.6% unemployment rate, a 64.1% participation rate, and a 60.6% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth eased to +4.7% in May, a 1.2-percentage-point deceleration from +5.9%71. The 5.6% unemployment rate is among the lowest of the large provinces, sitting below Ontario's 7.0% and British Columbia's 6.8% this period.
provinces.consumerPulse: Quebec CPI registered +1.5% year-over-year, the second-lowest provincial inflation rate this period — the inflation read71 accompanies wage growth of +4.7%, leaving pay changes running ahead of price changes for Quebec households. Building permits totalled $2.90B in April, up from $2.60B the prior period.

Hydro-Quebec's Action Plan 2035 and five wind partnerships anchor power-sector exposure, while the $10B Canada-Quebec transfer drives rate-sensitive transit.

provinces.name: Alberta
provinces.analysis:
Alberta posted the highest provincial participation rate at 69.1% and a lowest-tier CPI of +1.1% in the latest prints, with unemployment at 6.6% — wage growth71 decelerated to +4.8% in May, down 1.7 percentage points from +6.5%. GDP growth of +2.7% sits alongside 700 tracked Alberta projects, of which 176 qualify above the $200M threshold and total roughly $416.8B15.

Canada and Alberta signed an MOU announced 2026-05-15 covering a proposed bitumen-to-Asia pipeline, the Pathways Alliance carbon capture project, and a nuclear strategy, a package described as more than $126B in investment — the MOU58 sets a 2026-07-01 deadline for Alberta to submit a proposal for a pipeline of at least 1M bbl/day to the federal Major Projects Office, and resets the Pathways CCUS target to 16 megatonnes per year, a 77% reduction from the 68 Mt/yr figure announced in 2021. The Pathways Alliance CCS Hub Phase 1 ($16.5B, Proposed) ranks among the largest tracked power_energy files15.

Two C$50.0B proposed files anchor the top of Alberta's tracked pipeline — the Peace River Nuclear Power Project and the Olds AI Data Centre Hub (capped) — power_energy (161 files), government (141) and infrastructure (104) lead by count15, and WTI and WCS price movements flow through to oil-sands and CCUS capital plans. Housing starts fell 4.9% to 46,064 units SAAR as of June 15.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and energy lead Alberta's tracked count at 161 files, with the Pathways CCUS hub and two C$50.0B nuclear and data-centre files at the top of the pipeline — the database records 161 power_energy, 141 government and 104 infrastructure projects2. The proposed bitumen-to-Asia pipeline (at least 1M bbl/day) carries oil-price and export-differential exposure, while the $19.0B Telus province-wide telecom program and $12.0B Wonder Valley AI data centre park add capital-cost and power-demand sensitivity3.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Alberta carried the highest provincial participation rate at 69.1%, a 64.6% employment rate, and a 6.6% unemployment rate in the June LFS — wage growth eased to +4.8% in May, a 1.7-percentage-point deceleration from +6.5%71. The 69.1% participation rate leads all provinces, reflecting the province's energy and construction labour base.
provinces.consumerPulse: Alberta CPI ran at +1.1% year-over-year, in the lowest tier of provincial inflation this period — the inflation read71 accompanies wage growth of +4.8%, leaving pay changes well ahead of price changes for Alberta households. Building permits totalled $1.63B in April, up from $1.58B the prior period.
provinces.marketContext: Alberta's pipeline spans 700 tracked projects, with 176 qualifying above the $200M threshold totalling ~$416.8B; power_energy (161), government (141) and infrastructure (104) lead by count. WTI and WCS movements flow through to oil-sands and the Pathways Alliance CCS Hub, while the proposed bitumen-to-Asia pipeline carries oil-price and export-differential exposure.
provinces.tradeExposure: Alberta exports crude oil, bitumen, and natural gas with heavy U.S. and emerging Asian-market exposure; the proposed >=1M bbl/day bitumen-to-Asia pipeline and Pathways CCUS hub tie capital decisions to WTI, WCS, and export differentials.

provinces.name: Saskatchewan
provinces.analysis:
Saskatchewan posted the second-highest provincial GDP growth at +3.4% and a lowest-tier CPI of +1.1%, while housing starts fell 17.6% to 4,472 units SAAR, the sharpest provincial decline this period — the housing drop71 contrasts with a qualifying pipeline concentrated in potash mining rather than residential construction. The database tracks 154 Saskatchewan projects, of which 48 qualify above the $45M threshold and total roughly $52.9B15.

BHP booked a $2.3B impairment on the Jansen potash mine, citing cost and timing overruns on the Stage 2 expansion — the impairment52 leaves Jansen Stage 1 on track for first production mid-2027 at projected combined output of 8.5 Mtpa, roughly 10% of global potash, at the lowest unit cost among Canadian potash mines (US$114-130/t). Jansen Potash Project (C$13.9B, Under Construction) is the province's largest tracked file, and CN announced rail service on 2026-06-05 to connect Jansen production to global markets48.

Infrastructure, power, and mining lead Saskatchewan's tracked count at 41, 28, and 27 files respectively — potash prices drive the Jansen capital program (C$13.9B Under Construction, plus the $6.9B Stage 2 expansion that just absorbed a $2.3B impairment)15, while the proposed C$8.6B Thor alumina facility adds aluminum and commodity-price exposure. Wage growth eased to +4.1% in May, down 0.4 percentage points.

provinces.name: Nova Scotia
provinces.analysis:

Bear Head Energy ($8.0B, Proposed) is the largest tracked file15.

Defence and shipbuilding anchor the province's pipeline alongside the offshore-wind build-out — the Canadian Submarine Program (Hanwha Ocean proposal, $6.3B, Proposed) and Canadian Naval Radar Procurement ($2.5B, Proposed) are tracked alongside the roughly $70B, 30-year Irving Shipbuilding combat-vessel program11. goodsIndustries.name: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing & Hunting
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector GDP fell 1.1% month-over-month in the March 2026 reference period while holding up 2.1% year-over-year — the split reading84 tracks two sub-sectors moving in opposite directions, with the Saskatchewan farm canola price at $672.81 per tonne, unchanged on the week but up 1.8% month-over-month and 6.2% year-over-year.77 China cut its combined anti-dumping and countervail tariff on Canadian canola seed to roughly 14.9% effective March 1, 2026, down from a combined level near 84%, restoring access for approximately $4B per year of seed exports after China's 2025 canola imports fell nearly 50% under the prior tariffs.37

Forestry contracted as 21 permanent or indefinite British Columbia and Canada mill closures since 2023 removed roughly 15,000 forest-sector jobs since 2022 — Domtar permanently closed its Crofton, BC NBSK pulp facility (about 350 employees), even as lumber futures settled at $633.00, up 2.2% on the week and 6.4% over the month.4574 The potash and fertilizer proxy Nutrien traded at $88.73, down 6.2% on the week and 8.4% over the month, a softer input-cost signal for grain growers.77

The project database tracks 734 combined agriculture and forestry records carrying roughly $8.2B in pipeline value — about 269 of those records sit in forestry and hold $4.7B.24 If China's reduced canola tariff holds through 2026, the roughly $4B per year seed export channel would remain open for Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba growers.37

Arts, entertainment and recreation output rose 2.0% month-over-month and 3.5% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period, the strongest monthly gain of any industry — information, culture, and recreation employment rose 19,000 in May, up 2.3% month-over-month, coinciding with the sector's top-ranked monthly GDP move.8367 Scotia Place in Calgary reached its final-pile milestone, an NHL, WHL, NLL, and AHL venue with a community rink and retail.63

The project database tracks 322 tourism and culture records valued at roughly $22.0B, with one first-tracked since June 13 — a C$1.5B stadium project is planned for Halifax for a potential CFL franchise, another city is pursuing a C$94M arena, and Calgary Stampede Park's 20-year master plan includes seven zones.6327 Recreation demand tracks consumer spending and tourism; if arena and stadium projects advance through their milestones, the $22.0B tourism and culture pipeline would continue supporting the sector's elevated growth rate.27

servicesIndustries.name: Accommodation & Food Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Accommodation and food services output fell 0.4% month-over-month but ran 0.5% above year-ago levels against the March 2026 reference period — accommodation and food employment rose 17,000 in May, up 1.5% month-over-month, against a 3.8% job-vacancy rate recorded in 2024, roughly 18,230 unfilled positions versus 3.1% across all industries.8314 Tourism visitor spending is forecast at $140.9B in 2026, up 6% from 2025 on domestic, US, and overseas demand, growing faster than the wider economy.14

No discrete accommodation and food tag exists; activity is captured within the tourism_culture project bucket under NAICS 71 — the sector employs roughly 2.1 million people, and Ontario accommodation and food employed 426,700 in 2023, 37.8% of the national sector.1427 Demand tracks tourism, business travel, and consumer spending; if the projected 6% tourism-spending growth materializes, accommodation and food labour demand would stay elevated against an already-tight vacancy rate.27

servicesIndustries.analysis:
Public administration output rose 0.4% month-over-month and 1.1% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period — the 2026-27 Main Estimates total $502.8B in budgetary spending, $230.4B voted and $272.4B statutory, with transfer payments at 59.8% or $300.5B.831 The Spring Economic Update sets priorities of $25B for housing, $30B for defence, $115B for infrastructure, and $110B for productivity over five years, alongside $60B in spending reductions.1

The project database tracks 286 government and defence records valued at roughly $146.2B, with 10 first-tracked since June 13 — defence procurement this period includes the $39B Canada Submarine Fleet Replacement (Proposed), the $2.5B Far North Early Warning Arctic Radar in NT, and the $2.5B Canadian Naval Radar in NS.127 Public-administration capital tracks government budgets and policy priorities; if the submarine and Arctic-radar programs advance from Proposed status, the $146.2B pipeline would continue expanding through the procurement cycle.27

commodity_commentary: Commodity markets posted a mixed week as energy fell further while precious and base metals eased from recent highs — WTI fell 6.39% on the week to US$75.43/bbl and Brent fell 4.75% to US$79.28/bbl, an unwind of the supply-shock premium that had carried crude above US$96/bbl a month earlier, leaving WTI down 21.92% over the month.9 Precious metals held their annual gains as gold settled at US$4,226.70/oz, up 24.69% year-over-year, and silver at US$66.58/oz, up 85.07% year-over-year — the steepest 52-week percentage advance of any commodity tracked here, against a 52-week low of US$35.70/oz.9 Base metals were steady with copper at US$6.38/lb, near its 52-week high of US$6.58/lb and up 31.79% year-over-year, on sustained Chinese industrial demand after the May NBS Manufacturing PMI printed 50.0.59 Prairie staples were mixed: wheat rose to US$609.25/bu (+3.92% on the week, +7.31% year-over-year) while the StatCan canola farm price registered CAD$733.20/t for the May reference, its 52-week high.77 Lumber rose 0.32% to US$633.00/mfbm, up 8.11% over the month.9 The Signal Dispatch cross-reference engine ties commodity moves to 551 active Canadian mining projects ($199.9B aggregate) and 91 oil and gas projects ($63.2B).9
consumer_pulse:
Cost-of-living pressure framed the consumer picture, with headline CPI at +2.8% y/y while average hourly wage fell 1.4% m/m to $37.24 in May — April component detail recorded food +3.8% y/y and shelter +1.8% y/y, and the new housing price index eased 0.4% m/m to 121.1, its first negative print after flat-to-rising months.647074 The 5-year Government of Canada yield at 3.04% sets the mortgage-renewal anchor.

Energy costs eased over the month as WTI crude fell to $75.43/bbl from $96.60 a month earlier, lowering a gasoline-relevant input — by contrast, April energy CPI ran 28.6% above year-ago levels.6468 The household savings rate stood at 3.5% in Q1 2026, down 0.2 percentage points from 3.7%, with disposable income up 0.6% q/q; the 2-year Government of Canada yield at 2.76%, down 22 bps y/y, lowers the GIC anchor.82

Labour and fiscal signals rounded out the picture across the hard data stack — accommodation and food employment rose 4.3% m/m against retail down 1.8% m/m, while the federal Spring Economic Update 2026 committed $51B in infrastructure, a sovereign fund, and a CCUS-EOR tax-credit expansion.672 Housing starts rose to 279,317 SAAR in May, up 6.9% from the April pace, while the new housing price index eased 0.4% m/m to 121.1.7444 A CUSMA review remains open alongside tariff threats referenced in the prior edition.55

Canada Unemployment Rate — 12 Months Through May 2026
Source: Statistics Canada Labour Force Survey (14-10-0287). Monthly seasonally adjusted unemployment rate, June 2025 through May 2026.

May 2026 unemployment fell to 6.6% from 6.9% in April, the largest single-month decline in the 12-month window. The cross-reference engine links the sectoral pattern (construction +27K, transportation +19K, manufacturing +15K) to 964 active infrastructure projects ($200.04B), 468 transport/transit projects ($34.41B), and 79 manufacturing projects ($69.46B) — 1,511 active projects valued at $303.91B.

WTI Crude vs Western Canadian Heavy Oil Breakeven ($65/bbl Upper Bound)
Source: WTI front-month (CL=F) via yfinance, March 30 through May 19, 2026. Breakeven upper bound from public Western Canadian heavy oil greenfield project filings.

WTI closed at $92.00/bbl on June 8, down 10.7% from the May 19 baseline of $103.02 but still 41.5% above the $65/bbl upper bound of the Western Canadian heavy oil greenfield breakeven cohort. The cross-reference engine links current pricing to 35 active oil and gas projects ($56.53B) and 164 LNG, pipeline, and natural-gas-keyword projects ($167.51B).

CAD/USD Exchange Rate — 8 Weeks Through May 19, 2026
Source: CAD/USD daily close via yfinance, March 30 through May 19, 2026. June 7 WebSearch intraweek high of USD/CAD 1.3949 (CAD/USD 0.7169) cited in narrative.

CAD/USD declined from a 0.7351 peak on May 6 to 0.7264 on May 19 in the cached series, with the WebSearch June 7 print at 0.7169 (USD/CAD 1.3949). The cross-reference engine links the 200 bps BoC-Fed differential and the dollar move to 164 LNG, pipeline and natural-gas projects ($167.51B) carrying USD-denominated revenue streams that gain in CAD terms as the loonie weakens.

Government of Canada 2Y vs 10Y Yields — 6 Months Through May 19, 2026
GoC 10YGoC 2Y
Source: Government of Canada benchmark bond yields, December 1, 2025 through May 19, 2026. 2Y from goc_2y_yield, 10Y from goc_10y_yield (Bank of Canada).

The GoC 2s10s spread narrowed to 58 bps on May 19 from 70 bps in the prior edition, with the 2Y at 3.07% and the 10Y at 3.70%. The cross-reference engine links the 5-year fixed mortgage benchmark to 231 active residential projects ($36.27B), and the 10-year tenor to 164 LNG and natural gas projects ($167.51B) whose financing costs anchor to long-end yields.

yieldCurveCommentary: The Government of Canada yield curve held a normal slope with the 2s10s spread at +64 basis points — the 10Y benchmark sat at 3.40% versus the 2Y at 2.76%, following the Bank of Canada's June 10 decision to hold the overnight rate at 2.25% for the second consecutive meeting alongside the June Monetary Policy Report.28 Year-over-year the 2Y has risen 5 basis points from 2.71%, the 5Y 8 basis points from 2.96% to 3.04%, the 10Y 3 basis points from 3.37%, and the long bond 17 basis points from 3.65% to 3.82%, a steeper back-end term-premium pickup than at the front.9 The 5Y benchmark at 3.04% remains the residential mortgage-renewal anchor cited in the June MPR.29 The Signal Dispatch cross-reference engine ties the curve to 1,862 active rate-sensitive Canadian projects ($284.3B aggregate) financed against the GoC term structure, with 272 residential projects ($41.6B) most directly exposed to 5Y pricing for mortgage refinancing.9 If the 5Y benchmark holds above three percent through the third quarter, the 272 residential projects would face renewal pricing 8 basis points wider than the year-ago benchmark, while the broader rate-sensitive book priced off the 10Y would carry roughly 3 basis points of additional cost versus the same window in 2025.9

marketCommentary:
Crude oil retreated into the Canadian oil-sands breakeven band while equities held flat since the last edition — WTI crude fell to $75.43/bbl, down 6.4% from the prior edition's baseline10, settling inside the $74-76 breakeven cluster the cross-reference engine cites for 91 active oil and gas projects ($63.2B)10. The S&P/TSX Composite traded at 34,969, up 0.1%, and the S&P 500 stood at 7,501, up 0.5% over the same span10. The Canadian dollar eased 1.3% to 0.7066 CAD/USD as the Bank of Canada's overnight rate held at 2.25% following its June 10 decision28. The database tracks 6,485 active capital projects valued at $1,620.8B10.

Pipeline exposure splits along rate and commodity lines — 1,862 active rate-sensitive construction projects ($284.2B) finance against the Government of Canada curve, anchored by the 5-year benchmark at 3.04%, the mortgage-renewal reference28. If WTI holds at or below the $74-76 band, the 91 oil and gas projects ($63.2B) would sit at the lower edge of their cited breakevens10. Copper eased 2.0% since the last edition to $6.38/lb, while remaining 35.6% above its year-ago level, against 551 active mining projects ($199.9B)10.
